subject: Economics
description: Covers WPI vs CPI, Base Years, Core Inflation, IIP, Eight Core Industries, and Stagflation.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the fundamental difference between the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) and the Consumer Price Index (CPI) in India?

options.option_text: WPI does not include services and measures prices at the producer/wholesale level, whereas CPI includes both goods and services at the retail level
WPI is published by the National Statistical Office (NSO), while CPI is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser
WPI gives the highest weightage to food articles, whereas CPI gives the highest weightage to manufactured goods
WPI is used by the RBI as the official benchmark for its inflation targeting framework, while CPI is used only for DA calculations

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) tracks changes in the prices of goods sold and traded in bulk by wholesale businesses to other businesses. Crucially, WPI strictly EXCLUDES services (like healthcare, education, transport). Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks the retail prices of goods AND services bought directly by consumers.
DECOY BUSTING: 
- Publishing bodies are reversed in option B: WPI is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser (Ministry of Commerce), while CPI is published by the NSO (Ministry of Statistics). 
- Weightages are reversed in option C: WPI's highest weightage is Manufactured Products (~64%), while CPI's highest weightage is Food and Beverages (~45%). 
- Policy anchor is reversed in option D: RBI uses CPI (not WPI) for its 4% inflation target since 2014 based on the Urjit Patel committee recommendations. 
EXAM INSIGHT: Because WPI excludes services and has a heavy manufacturing weight, it is highly sensitive to global commodity prices (like crude oil and metals), whereas CPI reflects domestic retail inflation.

questions.stem: What is the current base year used for calculating the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in India?
questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The base year for the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in India was revised in 2017 from 2004-05 to 2011-12. This revision aligned the WPI base year with the base years of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and the Index of Industrial Production (IIP).
DECOY BUSTING: 2004-05 was the old base year. 2015-16 and 2018-19 are not official base years for any major national macroeconomic index. Note that for the Consumer Price Index (CPI-Combined), the base year is 2012. 
EXAM INSIGHT: Updating base years is critical in macroeconomic statistics because the consumption basket changes over time (e.g., smartphones became essential after 2004). The government periodically updates the base year to ensure the basket of goods accurately reflects current economic reality, though the revision to a more recent base year (like 2022-23) is currently pending.

questions.stem: Core inflation is widely monitored by central banks because it provides a more accurate picture of underlying long-term price trends. How is core inflation calculated?

options.option_text: By excluding highly volatile components, specifically food and energy prices, from the headline inflation index
By measuring only the price changes of essential food items and agricultural commodities
By tracking the inflation rate strictly in the core manufacturing sector, excluding agriculture and services
By measuring inflation only in the top metropolitan cities of the country

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Core inflation strips out the most volatile components of the inflation basket—namely Food and Fuel/Energy. These items are subject to sudden, temporary supply shocks (like a bad monsoon destroying onion crops, or geopolitical crises spiking global crude oil prices). 
DECOY BUSTING: Measuring only food items would be tracking the exact opposite of core inflation (it would be food inflation). Tracking only manufacturing or metropolitan cities are completely fictional definitions of core inflation.
EXAM INSIGHT: "Headline inflation" is the total, unadjusted inflation number (the CPI-Combined in India). When headline inflation spikes due to a temporary vegetable shortage, but core inflation remains stable, the RBI usually avoids raising interest rates, because monetary policy cannot fix a temporary agricultural supply shock. Central banks focus on core inflation to guide long-term interest rate policy.

questions.stem: The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) measures the short-term changes in the volume of production of industrial products. Which sector has the highest weightage in the IIP?

options.option_text: Manufacturing
Mining
Electricity
Construction

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) tracks manufacturing activity in different sectors. It is divided into three broad sectors with the following approximate weightages: Manufacturing (77.63%), Mining (14.37%), and Electricity (7.99%). Therefore, Manufacturing dominates the index.
DECOY BUSTING: Construction is not a primary sector in the broad IIP classification (though cement/steel used in construction are captured in manufacturing). Mining and Electricity have significantly lower weights than Manufacturing.
EXAM INSIGHT: The IIP is released monthly by the National Statistical Office (NSO). Within the IIP, there is a sub-category called the "Index of Eight Core Industries" (Coal, Crude Oil, Natural Gas, Refinery Products, Fertilizers, Steel, Cement, and Electricity). These 8 core industries comprise about 40.27% of the total weight of the IIP, acting as a lead indicator for overall industrial performance.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In the context of the Index of Eight Core Industries, which component holds the HIGHEST weightage?

options.option_text: Refinery Products
Electricity
Steel
Coal

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Eight Core Industries are the foundational pillars of the economy, making up ~40.27% of the total IIP. Their weightages in descending order are: Refinery Products (28.04%), Electricity (19.85%), Steel (17.92%), Coal (10.33%), Crude Oil (8.98%), Natural Gas (6.88%), Cement (5.37%), and Fertilizers (2.63%). Refinery products lead because petroleum refining is India's largest industrial segment by value.
DECOY BUSTING: Electricity and Steel are the second and third highest, respectively. Coal is fourth. Fertilizers has the lowest weightage.
EXAM INSIGHT: This is a classic, highly-repeated question in UPSC and SSC exams. A common mnemonic to remember the eight industries is CCC-F-R-E-N-S (Coal, Crude oil, Cement, Fertilizers, Refinery products, Electricity, Natural gas, Steel). Knowing the highest (Refinery) and lowest (Fertilizers) is practically mandatory for competitive exams.

questions.stem: Which index is historically used by the Government of India to calculate the Dearness Allowance (DA) for its employees and pensioners?

options.option_text: CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW)
CPI for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL)
Wholesale Price Index (WPI)
CPI-Combined (CPI-C)

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) is specifically designed to measure the impact of price changes on the cost of living of working-class families in industrial centres. It is the official benchmark used to calculate Dearness Allowance (DA) for central government employees and industrial workers to compensate them for inflation.
DECOY BUSTING: CPI-AL is used to revise minimum wages for agricultural labourers. WPI is a producer-level index, useless for consumer cost-of-living adjustments. CPI-Combined is the RBI's inflation anchor, but DA calculation traditionally relies on the specific CPI-IW series.
EXAM INSIGHT: The CPI-IW is compiled and released by the Labour Bureau (an attached office under the Ministry of Labour & Employment), NOT by the NSO. Its base year was recently updated to 2016 (from 2001) to better reflect modern consumption patterns of industrial workers.

questions.stem: Stagflation is an economic phenomenon that contradicts the traditional Phillips Curve. It is characterized by:

options.option_text: High inflation, high unemployment, and stagnant economic growth occurring simultaneously
A sustained period of deflation accompanied by high economic growth
Rapid economic growth causing runaway hyperinflation
High inflation caused by a booming job market and excessive wage growth

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Stagflation is a portmanteau of "Stagnation" and "Inflation." It occurs when an economy faces sluggish growth and high unemployment (stagnation) while simultaneously suffering from high price levels (inflation). It contradicts the traditional Phillips Curve, which posits that inflation and unemployment have an inverse relationship (i.e., inflation should fall when unemployment is high).
DECOY BUSTING: Deflation with high growth is completely opposite to stagflation. High inflation caused by a booming job market describes typical demand-pull inflation (an overheating economy), not stagflation. 
EXAM INSIGHT: The term was popularized during the 1970s oil crisis, when the OPEC oil embargo caused a massive supply shock. The price of oil skyrocketed, driving up inflation (cost-push), while industries ground to a halt and laid off workers (stagnation). It is a nightmare for central banks because standard monetary tools cannot fix both problems simultaneously (cutting rates fixes unemployment but worsens inflation).

questions.stem: The 'food and beverages' group carries the single largest weight in India's Consumer Price Index (Combined, base 2012). Approximately what is that weight?

options.option_text: Approximately 25%, reflecting urban household spending surveys
Approximately 36%, with cereals and pulses as the dominant driver
Approximately 46%, as food remains the largest expenditure category
Approximately 55%, combining rural and urban food consumption data

questions.explanation: Food and beverages account for 45.86% (~46%) of the CPI-Combined basket (2012 base), reflecting the dominant share of food in Indian household budgets. Option B (36%) is a tempting guess because urban households spend less on food than rural ones, but the combined rural-urban basket pushes the share considerably higher.

questions.stem: India's Consumer Price Index (Combined) was originally launched with a 2010 base but was subsequently revised. What is the base year currently used for this CPI series?

options.option_text: 2004–05, the base adopted in the pre-revision WPI framework
2010, the original base when the new CPI-Combined series was introduced
2012, the current base year following revision of the earlier series
2011–12, chosen to align with the National Accounts Statistics revision

questions.explanation: The CPI-Combined series was launched in 2011 initially with 2010=100, but was revised to 2012=100, which is the current base year. Option B (2010) is the most common mistake because it was the original base — the revision to 2012 is frequently tested. Option D (2011-12) is the WPI base year, not CPI.

questions.stem: Under the Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework operationalised in India in 2016, what is the official inflation target and permissible tolerance band mandated for the Monetary Policy Committee?

options.option_text: 3.5% target with ±1% band, set in consultation with the Finance Ministry
4% target with ±2% band, as officially notified by the Government of India
5% target with ±2% band, anchored to the upper range of the WPI trajectory
4.5% target with ±1.5% band, mirroring the international median inflation target

questions.explanation: Under Section 45ZA of the RBI Act (as amended in 2016), the Government notified a CPI inflation target of 4% with a tolerance band of ±2% (lower bound 2%, upper bound 6%). Breaching either bound for three consecutive quarters triggers a mandatory explanation from the MPC to the Government. Option D (4.5%) is often confused because it appeared in earlier RBI guidance notes before the formal FIT adoption.

questions.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes the GDP Deflator from the Consumer Price Index (CPI) as a measure of economy-wide inflation?

options.option_text: CPI tracks only urban prices while GDP Deflator spans both urban and rural areas
GDP Deflator uses current-period output quantities as weights, making it a Paasche-type index
CPI is published annually by MoSPI while GDP Deflator is released monthly by the RBI
GDP Deflator excludes import prices while CPI includes imported consumer goods costs

questions.explanation: The GDP Deflator implicitly uses current-period quantities (a Paasche-type approach) because it is derived from nominal vs real GDP, both measured at current production composition. CPI uses a fixed base-year basket (Laspeyres). Option D contains a grain of truth — the GDP Deflator covers domestically produced output, so pure imports affect it differently — but the defining structural difference is the quantity-weighting method, making B the best answer.

questions.stem: A central bank report states: 'The year-on-year rate of price increase has moderated from 8.2% to 4.9% over the past 12 months.' Which economic term precisely describes this development?

options.option_text: Deflation, since consumer prices have declined relative to the previous year
Reflation, a deliberate policy action to stimulate a contracting economy
Disinflation, a fall in the inflation rate while prices still rise overall
Hyperinflation, an uncontrolled extreme acceleration of general price levels

questions.explanation: Disinflation means the rate of inflation is declining — prices are still rising, just more slowly. Here prices rose at 4.9%, not fell, so it is not deflation (which requires a negative rate). Option A (deflation) is the most common wrong answer: students confuse 'slowing inflation' with 'falling prices'. Reflation is a policy response to deflation, not a description of this scenario.

questions.stem: As per the RBI Act, 1934 (Section 45ZB), inserted by the 2016 amendment, the Monetary Policy Committee has six members. Which option correctly states its composition and the tie-breaking provision?

options.option_text: Three RBI members and three Finance Ministry nominees; tie broken by Finance Secretary
Three RBI officials and three government-appointed external experts; RBI Governor breaks ties
Four RBI members and two government nominees; minimum of five votes required for a decision
Two RBI members and four government-appointed experts; Finance Secretary holds the casting vote

questions.explanation: Section 45ZB specifies: (i) RBI Governor, (ii) the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, (iii) one RBI officer nominated by the Central Board — plus three external members nominated by the Central Government. Decisions are by majority (4 of 6 needed); in a tie, the RBI Governor casts a second, deciding vote. Option A wrongly attributes the casting vote to the Finance Secretary, which would compromise MPC independence — a nuance frequently tested.

questions.stem: The Laspeyres price index formula used in India's WPI and CPI is widely acknowledged to impart an upward bias in measured inflation. What is the primary reason for this systematic overstatement?

options.option_text: It overweights falling-price goods by anchoring basket shares to current-year quantities
It ignores quality improvements in products, causing understatement of real living-standard gains
It fixes base-period quantities, missing consumer substitution toward relatively cheaper goods
It assigns equal weight to all commodities regardless of their actual expenditure shares

questions.explanation: The Laspeyres formula holds base-period quantities constant. When prices of some goods rise, real consumers substitute toward cheaper alternatives — but the index still values the old, pricier basket, overstating the true cost of maintaining the same utility. This is called substitution bias. Option A describes the Paasche index's tendency (which can understate). Option B refers to quality-adjustment bias, a separate issue identified by the Boskin Commission — it affects CPI accuracy but operates differently from substitution bias.
